frames.narration: A search box echoes input unescaped, so an attacker has put 4 things into the page: an inline script, an onerror handler, a script from their own server, and a script through an allowed CDN. With no policy, the browser runs all 4 and loads all 11 legitimate resources.

The first fix people reach for: an allow-list of hosts, plus 'unsafe-inline' because the page uses inline code. The script from evil.example is blocked, but the inline script and the handler run, and so does the one through the allowed CDN. 3 of 4 still run.

Drop 'unsafe-inline': now only 1 injected script runs, the one through the allowed CDN host. But the page's own inline code is blocked too, and only 7 of the 11 needed resources load. The page is half broken.

A nonce policy: the server makes a fresh random nonce for this response, writes it in the header and on its own script tags, and adds strict-dynamic. Scripts without the nonce do not run, so all 4 injected scripts are blocked, and 10 of the 11 needed resources load. Only the old inline onclick handler breaks, because nonces do not cover handler attributes.

Break it: the developer caches the page, so the same nonce goes out on every response. The attacker has seen it, copies it onto the injected scripts, and 3 of 4 run again. The nonce only works while it is unguessable and used once.

Rollout: before enforcing, send the same policy as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only. Nothing is blocked and the page works as before, but every violation is reported, so you see what you would have broken.

Fix the reports (rewrite the onclick handler as an event listener, add the nonce to third-party tags), then enforce. Add the one-line headers as well: frame-ancestors, nosniff, HSTS and SameSite cookies each stop one more attack, and 4 of 4 together stop all four in the toy list.
